prompt: Analyze Aristotle's theory of perception and the common sense (koinē aisthēsis) in De Anima III, with attention to how phantasia mediates between perception and thought.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthēsis

Aristotle's account of φαντασία in *De Anima* III is grounded in the prior operation of sense-perception, such that the image-making faculty cannot function independently of αἴσθησις; yet phantasia is emphatically not reducible to perception itself. As Aristotle defines the perceptual faculty, "all sense-perception is a process of being so affected; so that that which makes something such as it itself actually is makes the other such because the other is already potentially such" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 36–37). Perception thus constitutes a transition from potentiality to actuality through the agency of an external sensible object, receiving sensible forms without matter. Phantasia, however, emerges as a secondary motion consequent upon this primary actuality: an "appearing" (phainetai) that may occur even "when the sense-powers are inoperative, as in dreams or when one's eyes are closed, so that phantasia cannot be the same thing as sensation" (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). Accordingly, the decisive contrast between phantasia and aisthēsis lies precisely in their divergent conditions of operation; perception requires the present engagement of a sensible object, whereas phantasia persists in its absence. Nevertheless, White observes that "phantasia seems not to occur without sensation, since both take place in the same subjects and are directed to the same objects" (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). This causal dependency upon sensation, paired with functional autonomy from it, generates a productive tension—one that Aristotle never fully resolves—between phantasia's derivative origin and its independent cognitive operations in dreaming, deliberation, and memory. Frede reports that Aristotle defines phantasia as a motion arising from sense-perception's activity that resembles perception yet remains distinct from it (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 6). The question of phantasia's internal grades—its sensory and deliberative varieties, its complex relation to belief (doxa), and the degree to which it admits of voluntary control—will be addressed more fully in the sections that follow.

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia

The relationship between φαντασία as a faculty or capacity and the φάντασμα as its product—the image or residual sensory impression—constitutes a crucial articulation within Aristotle's psychology of cognition. Aristotle asserts directly that "to the thinking soul images serve as if they were contents of perception (and when it asserts or denies them to be good or bad it avoids or pursues them)" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 47–48). The phantasma thus occupies a mediating position: it is neither the immediate deliverances of sense nor the fully discursive content of νοῦς, but rather a quasi-perceptual representation that the intellect takes up in lieu of sensory presence. Indeed, (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in *Movement of Animals*, "thinking and imagination produce that which brings about the affections, since they produce the forms which bring them about" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). Phantasmata are therefore not merely passive residues; they function as active forms capable of initiating physiological and psychological change. Frede underscores this point by arguing that phantasia endows the object of perception with formal content that exceeds what mere after-images can supply, noting the difficulty of explaining how a psychological process that is "nothing but a secondary motion ensuing upon sense-perception" could fulfill the wider interpretive function Aristotle assigns to it (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 6). Papachristou similarly prefers to leave the Greek word "phantasia" untranslated, precisely because the English "imagination" fails to capture the technical range Aristotle intends (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). The distinction between sensory phantasia—which produces phantasmata closely tied to particular perceptions—and deliberative phantasia—which combines and reconfigures images in service of practical reasoning—thus marks an essential internal differentiation. The question of phantasia's voluntariness similarly emerges here: while deliberative phantasia admits a degree of rational control, sensory phantasmata often arise unbidden, particularly in states of sleep or passion; Frede notes that "the uncontrolled status of phantasiai as after-images" aligns with a non-committal, sceptical reading of the faculty (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 5).

## 3. Phantasia and Mnēmē

The relationship between φαντασία and μνήμη reveals a further dimension of phantasia's mediating role, for memory depends essentially upon the persistence of phantasmata across time. Aristotle establishes this dependency explicitly: "all memory implies a time elapsed; consequently only those animals which perceive time remember, and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1). Memory thus presupposes both perceptual experience and the temporal awareness that accompanies it; yet the content that memory retains is not the original perception itself but rather the phantasma—the residual image or impression left by perception's actualization. Accordingly, mnēmē belongs to the primary faculty of sense-perception not as a species of aisthēsis but as a subsequent dispositional state conditioned by the lapse of time and directed exclusively at the past. Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle's psychology illuminates this structure further; perceiving is characterized as "πάσχειν, affected by beings as world; πάσχειν as δέχεσθαι, 'to perceive' and that primarily as πάθος, 'becoming-affected,' 'disposition,' being related to the world as in it, being in dealings with it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). Memory, on this account, preserves the dispositional residue of such being-affected, retaining the πάθος in the form of a phantasma that can be subsequently recalled. The tension between phantasia's causal derivation from sensation and its functional autonomy in memory is thus particularly acute: the phantasma that constitutes memory's content originated in perception but now operates independently of any present sensible object. Whether sensory or deliberative, phantasia in its mnemonic function illustrates that the faculty sustains cognitive life well beyond the moment of perceptual encounter; the relation to doxa and voluntary control in this domain will be elaborated below.

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa

Aristotle's careful separation of φαντασία from δόξα in *De Anima* III.3 reveals the distinctive epistemic status of imagination as a faculty that generates appearances without committing the soul to propositional belief. While doxa involves conviction (pistis) and is subject to rational evaluation as true or false, phantasia operates beneath and alongside judgment; one may entertain a phantasma of something fearful while simultaneously holding the belief that no danger is present. Frede highlights this asymmetry by noting that the "uncontrolled status of phantasiai as after-images justifies" an interpretation of phantasia as corresponding to "a sceptical, cautious, and non-committing phainetai" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 5). Thus phantasia produces an appearing that need not carry the doxastic force of assertion or denial; yet Aristotle also acknowledges that doxa can arise from phantasia, particularly in cases where emotional response precedes discursive reasoning. The practical implications are significant: in the *Movement of Animals*, (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) thinking and imagination "produce the forms which bring about" affections and bodily movements (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11), suggesting that phantasia's influence on action can bypass the deliberative mediation of doxa entirely. White's analysis confirms that establishing "the precise relation" between phantasia and other cognitive faculties—perception, belief, knowledge—remains the central interpretive challenge of *De Anima* III.3 (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). The distinction between sensory phantasia, which operates independently of belief, and deliberative phantasia, which cooperates with rational calculation, thus marks the boundary along which phantasia and doxa interact without collapsing into identity; indeed, it is precisely phantasia's capacity to generate appearances that are neither believed nor disbelieved that renders it indispensable to Aristotle's account of how perception mediates toward thought.
